section.heading: 5.3 Diagonalization
section.paragraph: In many cases, the eigenvalue–eigenvector information contained within a matrix $$A$$ can be displayed in a useful factorization of the form $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ where $$D$$ is a diagonal matrix. In this section, the factorization enables us to compute $$A^{k}$$ quickly for large values of $$k$$ , a fundamental idea in several applications of linear algebra. Later, in Sections 5.6 and 5.7, the factorization will be used to analyze (and decouple) dynamical systems.
The following example illustrates that powers of a diagonal matrix are easy to compute.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$D = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$D^{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and
$$D^{3} = D D^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{3} \end{bmatrix}$$
In general,
$$D^{k} = \begin{bmatrix} 5^{k} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{k} \end{bmatrix} \text{for} k \geq 1$$

section.paragraph: If $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ for some invertible $$P$$ and diagonal $$D$$ , then $$A^{k}$$ is also easy to compute, as the next example shows.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 7 & 2 \\ {- 4} & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find a formula for $$A^{k}$$ , given that $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , where
$$P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The standard formula for the inverse of a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix yields
$$P^{- 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
Then, by associativity of matrix multiplication,

$$A^{2} & = & \left(\right. P D P^{- 1} \left.\right) \left(\right. P D P^{- 1} \left.\right) = P D \underset{I}{\underset{︸}{\left(\right. P^{- 1} P \left.\right)}} D P^{- 1} = P D D P^{- 1} & = & P D^{2} P^{- 1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Again,
$$A^{3} = \left(\right. P D P^{- 1} \left.\right) A^{2} = \left(\right. P D \underset{I}{\underset{︸}{P^{- 1} \left.\right) P}} D^{2} P^{- 1} = P D D^{2} P^{- 1} = P D^{3} P^{- 1}$$
In general, for $$k \geq 1$$ ,

$$A^{k} & = P D^{k} P^{- 1} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5^{k} & 0 \\ 0 & 3^{k}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 \cdot 5^{k} - 3^{k} & 5^{k} - 3^{k} \\ 2 \cdot 3^{k} - 2 \cdot 5^{k} & 2 \cdot 3^{k} - 5^{k}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

section.paragraph: A square matrix $$A$$ is said to be diagonalizable if $$A$$ is similar to a diagonal matrix, that is, if $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ for some invertible matrix $$P$$ and some diagonal matrix $$D$$ . The next theorem gives a characterization of diagonalizable matrices and tells how to construct a suitable factorization.

note.title: Theorem ﻿5
note.heading: Theorem ﻿5
The Diagonalization Theorem﻿
note.paragraph: An $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is diagonalizable if and only if $$A$$ has $$n$$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

In fact, $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , with $$D$$ a diagonal matrix, if and only if the columns of $$P$$ are $$n$$ linearly independent eigenvectors of $$A$$ . In this case, the diagonal entries of $$D$$ are eigenvalues of $$A$$ that correspond, respectively, to the eigenvectors in $$P$$ .

section.paragraph: In other words, $$A$$ is diagonalizable if and only if there are enough eigenvectors to form a basis of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . We call such a basis an eigenvector basis of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: First, observe that if $$P$$ is any $$n \times n$$ matrix with columns $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ , and if $$D$$ is any diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ , then
$$A P = A \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{v}_{1} & \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A \textbf{v}_{1} & A \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & A \textbf{v}_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$
while

$$P D = P \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{1} & 0 & \hdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_{2} & \hdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \hdots & \lambda_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} & \lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & \lambda_{n} \textbf{v}_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$
Now suppose $$A$$ is diagonalizable and $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ . Then right-multiplying this relation by $$P$$ , we have $$AP = PD$$ . In this case, equations (1) and (2) imply that

$$\begin{bmatrix} A \textbf{v}_{1} & A \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & A \textbf{v}_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} & \lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & \lambda_{n} \textbf{v}_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$
Equating columns, we find that
$$A \textbf{v}_{1} = \lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} , A \textbf{v}_{2} = \lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} , \ldots , A \textbf{v}_{n} = \lambda_{n} \textbf{v}_{n}$$

Since $$P$$ is invertible, its columns $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ must be linearly independent. Also, since these columns are nonzero, the equations in (4) show that $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ are eigenvalues and $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ are corresponding eigenvectors. This argument proves the “only if” parts of the first and second statements, along with the third statement, of the theorem.

Finally, given any $$n$$ eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ , use them to construct the columns of $$P$$ and use corresponding eigenvalues $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ to construct $$D$$ . By equations (1)–(3), $$AP = PD$$ . This is true without any condition on the eigenvectors. If, in fact, the eigenvectors are linearly independent, then $$P$$ is invertible (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem), and $$AP = PD$$ implies that $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ .
section.heading: Diagonalizing Matrices

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Diagonalize the following matrix, if possible.
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ - 3 & - 5 & - 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
That is, find an invertible matrix $$P$$ and a diagonal matrix $$D$$ such that $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: There are four steps to implement the description in Theorem 5.

Step 1. Find the eigenvalues of $$\mathbf{\mathit{A}}$$ . As mentioned in Section 5.2, the mechanics of this step are appropriate for a computer when the matrix is larger than $$2 \times 2$$ . To avoid unnecessary distractions, the text will usually supply information needed for this step. In the present case, the characteristic equation turns out to involve a cubic polynomial that can be factored: $$0 = det ( A - \lambda I ) & = & - \lambda^{3} - 3 \lambda^{2} + 4 & = & - ( \lambda - 1 ) \left(( \lambda + 2 )\right)^{2}$$
The eigenvalues are $$\text{λ} = 1$$ and $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ .

Step 2. Find three linearly independent eigenvectors of $$\mathbf{\mathit{A}}$$ . Three vectors are needed because $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix. This is the critical step. If it fails, then Theorem 5 says that $$A$$ cannot be diagonalized. The method in Section 5.1 produces a basis for each eigenspace: $$\text{Basis} \text{for} \lambda & = & 1 ; v_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \text{Basis} \text{for} \lambda = - 2 ; v_{2} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \text{and} v_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
You can check that $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3}\}$$ is a linearly independent set.

Step 3. Construct $$\mathbf{\mathit{P}}$$ from the vectors in step 2. The vectors may be listed in any order. Using the order chosen in step 2, form $$P = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_{1} & \mathbf{v}_{2} & \mathbf{v}_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 4. Construct $$\mathbf{\mathit{D}}$$ from the corresponding eigenvalues. In this step, it is essential that the order of the eigenvalues matches the order chosen for the columns of $$P$$ . Use the eigenvalue $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ twice, once for each of the eigenvectors corresponding to $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ : $$D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

It is a good idea to check that $$P$$ and $$D$$ really work. To avoid computing $$P^{- 1}$$ , simply verify that $$AP = PD$$ . This is equivalent to $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ when $$P$$ is invertible. (However, be sure that $$P$$ is invertible!) Compute $$A P & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 3 & 3 \\ - 3 & - 5 & - 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ - 1 & - 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} P D & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 2 & 2 \\ - 1 & - 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Diagonalize the following matrix, if possible.
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 3 \\ - 4 & - 6 & - 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The characteristic equation of $$A$$ turns out to be exactly the same as that in Example 3:
$$0 = det \left(\right. A - \lambda I \left.\right) = - \lambda^{3} - 3 \lambda^{2} + 4 = - \left(\right. \lambda - 1 \left.\right) \left(\right. \lambda + 2 \left.\right)^{2}$$
The eigenvalues are $$\text{λ} = 1$$ and $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ . However, it is easy to verify that each eigenspace is only one-dimensional:

$$\text{Basis for} \lambda & = 1 : & \textbf{v}_{1} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \text{Basis for} \lambda & = - 2 : & \textbf{v}_{2} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

There are no other eigenvalues, and every eigenvector of $$A$$ is a multiple of either $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ or $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . Hence it is impossible to construct a basis of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ using eigenvectors of $$A$$ . By Theorem 5, $$A$$ is not diagonalizable.

section.paragraph: The following theorem provides a sufficient condition for a matrix to be diagonalizable.

note.title: Theorem 6
note.heading: Theorem 6
note.paragraph: An $$n \times n$$ matrix with $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ be eigenvectors corresponding to the $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues of a matrix $$A$$ . Then $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ is linearly independent, by Theorem 2 in Section 5.1. Hence $$A$$ is diagonalizable, by Theorem 5.

It is not necessary for an $$n \times n$$ matrix to have $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues in order to be diagonalizable. The $$3 \times 3$$ matrix in Example 3 is diagonalizable even though it has only two distinct eigenvalues.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Determine if the following matrix is diagonalizable.
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & - 8 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: This is easy! Since the matrix is triangular, its eigenvalues are obviously $$5$$ , $$0$$ , and $$- 2$$ . Since $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with three distinct eigenvalues, $$A$$ is diagonalizable.

section.heading: Matrices Whose Eigenvalues Are Not Distinct
section.paragraph: If an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ has $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues, with corresponding eigenvectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{n},$$ and if $$P = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$P$$ is automatically invertible because its columns are linearly independent, by Theorem 2. When $$A$$ is diagonalizable but has fewer than $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues, it is still possible to build $$P$$ in a way that makes $$P$$ automatically invertible, as the next theorem shows.1

note.title: Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix whose distinct eigenvalues are $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{p}$$ .

list.item: For $$1 \leq k \leq p$$ , the dimension of the eigenspace for $$\text{λ} _{k}$$ is less than or equal to the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $$\text{λ} _{k}$$ .

The matrix $$A$$ is diagonalizable if and only if the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces equals $$n$$ , and this happens if and only if (i) the characteristic polynomial factors completely into linear factors and (ii) the dimension of the eigenspace for each $$\text{λ} _{k}$$ equals the multiplicity of $$\text{λ} _{k}$$ .

If $$A$$ is diagonalizable and $$B_{k}$$ is a basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $$\text{λ} _{k}$$ for each $$k$$ , then the total collection of vectors in the sets $$B_{1},\ldots,B_{p}$$ forms an eigenvector basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Diagonalize the following matrix, if possible.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Since $$A$$ is a triangular matrix, the eigenvalues are $$5$$ and $$- 3$$ , each with multiplicity $$2$$ . Using the method in Section 5.1, we find a basis for each eigenspace.

$$\text{Basis} \text{for} \lambda = 5 : & \mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 8 \\ 4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \begin{matrix} \text{and} & \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 16 \\ 4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix} \text{Basis} \text{for} \lambda = - 3 : & \mathbf{v}_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \begin{matrix} \text{and} & \mathbf{v}_{4} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix}$$

The set $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{4}\}$$ is linearly independent, by Theorem 7. So the matrix $$P =$$ $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is invertible, and $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , where

list.item: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {- 3} & 12 \\ {- 2} & 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Suppose you are told that $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are eigenvectors of $$A$$ . Use this information to diagonalize $$A$$ .

Let $$A$$ be a $$4 \times 4$$ matrix with eigenvalues $$5$$ , $$3$$ , and $$- 2$$ , and suppose you know that the eigenspace for $$\text{λ} = 3$$ is two-dimensional. Do you have enough information to determine if $$A$$ is diagonalizable?
